This assessment considers how spontaneous emission rates change when an initially excited atom is accelerated versus an atom at rest encountering a moving mirror.

A longstanding issue regarding massive star origins involves whether these stars always form within dense clusters and, if found in less crowded environments, if they inevitably moved there.  Recent advances in wide-scale photometric surveys enable us to detect massive stars without bias in the less crowded regions of the galaxy.  This study examines forty candidate OB stars discovered by Mohr-Smith et al in the vicinity of Westerlund 2, with locations confined to a 1.5 degree radius around the cluster.  By utilizing fossil records from Gaia and spectroscopic data from WISPs/IRSF, we have determined the masses of these stars, classifying thirty as O/N type, with the remainder being early B stars.  Initial analysis suggests ten stars initially lacked counterparts from Mohr-Smith et al's study, although the reasons for this discrepancy likely involve photometric confusion and temperature measurement inaccuracies.  Data on the distances of these stars show an overabundance of late O/B stars concentrated near Westerlund 2, in contrast to an evenly distributed early O star.  The study's findings imply the presence of young clusters or high-density regions within a 400 pc radius of Distante, which could be responsible for the formation of massive stars observed in the area.  Supra-association cluster formation patterns may contribute significantly to the general massive star population, with potential implications for our understanding of these stars' formation in the galaxy.

Degraded handwritten documents, which are susceptible to damage from paper ageing and environmental factors, can cause severe readability issues for current text recognition algorithms. To overcome these challenges, we propose an innovative, end-to-end approach utilizing Generative Adversarial Networks that not only restores visual clarity but also improves the overall readability of the documents. This pioneering method differs from conventional binarization techniques, which primarily focus on enhancing visual quality, by integrating a text recognition module to optimize generated output. The effectiveness of this architecture was validated through comprehensive experiments conducted on Arabic and Latin handwritten texts, showcasing improved readability and visual quality.

The growth of Information Technology has significantly altered how information is shared, making it necessary to convert printed documents into digital formats.  There has been an increase in fraudulent activities lately.  To prevent such account-related fraud, a system was devised which employs ID card extraction via OCR and NLP for verification purposes.  Optical Character Recognition, a technology that enables the conversion of images to text, can also be used to convert an Indonesian ID card or KTP into text format.  This facilitates easier data entry for service providers, while NLP is utilized to correct any inaccuracies resulting from the OCR process.  To improve extraction accuracy, both technologies can be combined.  Our extractor was successfully tested using 500 Indonesian ID card images and yielded an extraction accuracy of 98%.  Furthermore, our system has been implemented using a client-server architecture and can function as an standalone application.  Additionally, its user-friendly interface makes it accessible to anyone without technical expertise in OCR or NLP.

In vehicular communications, the complex and dispersive nature of channels makes reliable channel estimation vital for optimal system performance, yet the IEEE 802.11p standard's limited pilots lead to inadequate channel tracking. As a result, conventional IEEE 802.11p estimators experience significant performance decline, particularly in high-speed scenarios. To overcome these challenges, researchers have explored deep learning (DL) techniques for channel estimation in IEEE 802.11p. Nonetheless, these approaches either underperform in extremely high-speed situations or exhibit substantial computational complexities. To resolve these problems, this paper introduces an innovative solution based on a long short-term memory (LSTM) model for channel estimation. The proposed method incorporates an LSTM unit for channel estimation, followed by a temporal averaging technique to mitigate noise, and analytically calculates the noise mitigation ratio to verify its effectiveness. The experimental results demonstrate the proposed solution's capacity to surpass conventional IEEE 802.11p estimators, as well as its ability to remain adaptable in extremely high-speed scenarios while maintaining substantially lower computational requirements.

The task of automatically assigning colors to images without human involvement has garnered interest within the machine learning community for a limited time. Colorization is particularly challenging due to its inherently high degrees of freedom; when presented with an image, multiple plausible color combinations exist, and there may be no single definitive solution. Another related issue is Single Image Super Resolution, a task that involves converting low-resolution images into higher-resolution versions. This research targets a novel, automatic colorization approach, specializing in astronomical images and leveraging Generative Adversarial Networks. We propose a new loss function that maintains low-resolution features during high-resolution training and achieves favorable results on a limited dataset. Additionally, our method facilitates the creation of colored images from low-resolution, grayscale originals. This approach is successfully demonstrated on actual astronomical images, resulting in accurately colored outputs that align with experts' assessments.

We've developed a novel numerical scheme to efficiently calculate Artificial Neural Networks (ANN) weights without relying on tedious iterative processes. Based on the Universal Approximation Theorem, our proposed algorithm rapidly achieves low error rates in the regression and classification of intricate datasets, such as the Griewank function and the MNIST database for handwritten digits. Its mathematical formulation allows it to accurately approximate highly complex nonlinear functions with a minimal margin of error, and it also facilitates the solution of Partial Differential Equations. The approach works by determining the weights of individual neurons using analytical expressions that marginalize the nonlinearity of the activation function, thereby simplifying the weight calculation and enhancing the learning speed. Additionally, our method features enhanced generalization capabilities and exhibits a decline in the mean squared error that scales at a rate of O(1/N^(1/2))) as the number of training samples (N) increases.

The ECFA Early Career Researcher's panel started representing the interests of young researchers in the ECFA community in January 2021. Throughout its first two years of operation, the panel developed its organizational framework, cooperated with ECFA by offering input and insights, and introduced several projects focused on comprehending and addressing the varied needs of young researchers. This report outlines the details of the panel's formation and operations as well as its engagement with numerous activities during its first two years of operation.

Confining modes at the edge, known as line waves, can propagate on the boundary between two specially designed electromagnetic interfaces that maintain their electrical properties despite changes in thickness. These waves, characterized by sharp local variations in electric field, are confined both spatially and temporally. In this study, line waves are generated numerically using dual metasurfaces, consisting of two interfaces with different electrical properties. These metasurfaces are designed using fish-scale-like structures with inherent electrical symmetries broken. Line waves are found to radiate from critical points on the boundary, and their propagation can be controlled by modifying the line's geometry, as well as through changes in frequency and curvature. These properties make line waves suitable for various optical applications, such as directional emission, polarization generation, and beam manipulation.

One of the most effective approaches to building intelligent robotic systems is Learning from Demonstration (LfD), however research is still needed to overcome challenges such as multi-agent learning and prolonged autonomy.  A new architecture for multi-agent LfD is introduced which enables the creation of reliable and efficient robotic systems in complex and large-scale environments by leveraging advancements in Artificial Intelligence (AI) through the implementation of a Federated Learning (FL)-based collaborative learning environment involving both humans and robots. This novel approach integrates AI-driven cognitive robotics with AI-driven machine learning to address the lack of robust and robust AI foundations in LfD research, and as a result demonstrates the first FL-based implementation of multi-agent LfD successfully in a real-world scenario of joint human-robot object manipulation.

A new bias-corrected estimator has been created for the mean absolute deviation of a median, specifically designed for use with skewer data sets. The performance of this estimator is evaluated in terms of its ability to accurately estimate the median and the mean absolute deviation, both in ideal circumstances and when actually measured from simulated data sets. The results show that it performs better the more skewed the data, when compared to the original Koenker-Diehl estimator.

The tasks of relation extraction and knowledge graph link prediction share a
common link in their objectives, allowing them to complement each other in the
process of predicting a subject-object relationship in a sentence. Specifically,
when a model identifies an object and its related subject, this relationship can
be utilized by another model to anticipate a list of potential objects associated
with the subject, indicating the original object should also be included in the
list. In our study, we utilized this connection by implementing a multi-task
approach, training existing relation extraction models alongside knowledge graph
link prediction to ultimately boost the models' overall performance and achieve
predictable gains in accuracy.

The Analytical Exact Iteration Method has been employed to solve the N-dimensional Radial Schrödinger equation for complex-valued potentials, and further generalized to consider finite values of anisotropy, finite baryonic chemical potential, and Debye mass based on quasi-particle approach. Energy eigenvalues have been calculated in the N-dimensional Schrödinger framework. Binding energies of quarkonium states have been calculated and analyzed in terms of anisotropy, Debye mass, and baryonic chemical potential for different N values. It has been observed that increasing anisotropy, Debye mass, or baryonic chemical potential leads to the dissociation of quarkonium states at ground state in line with previous research, while anisotropy leads to the dissociation temperature rising compared to the case of isotropy. Anisotropy also causes the lead state to dissociate compared to the case of isotropy. Anisotropy, Debye mass, and baryonic chemical potential influence the quark movement which leads to the correction of the previous research result. An N-value of 3 has been picked up to compare with the physical case in the N-dimensional Schrödinger framework. An anisotropy, Debye mass, and baryonic chemical potential influence the quark movement which leads to the correction of the previous research result.

Our study focused on the magnetic arrangements within the crystals of Tb3RuO7 and Nd3RuO7 using neutron-diffraction experiments. In Tb3RuO7, neighboring ruthenium atoms created a chain pattern, with some being ordered magnetically and others remaining randomly aligned. This unique combination resulted in an intermediate disordered state, with the two ruthenium types exhibiting similar yet distinct behaviors. In Nd3RuO7, the magnetic patterns were uniform and independent for the two ruthenium species, with both being ordered at temperatures below 17.5 K. We attribute the disordered state in Tb3RuO7 primarily to the magnetic frustrations, caused by the differing internal magnetic fields imposed by the ordered terbium atoms on the two ruthenium species, leading to distinct behaviors.

Multi-Layer Perceptrons are particularly effective at generating accurate
low-dimensional representations of data, such as images, shapes and light
fields. Despite advancements using periodic activations or positional
encodings, they have historically been tailored to process a single signal
and sacrificed some degree of generality. We introduce an innovative new
approach to representation learning that not only generalizes well to multiple
signals, but outperforms the competition in fidelity. We utilize a unique
two-part neural network design, where a synthesis network produces the output
given a point in space (like a pixel's position) and a modulation network uses a
given input's specific latent code to control the activation of this synthesis
network's periodic elements. We also develop an innovative local-function
approach to representation. It divides the input domain into uniform squares,
and each one has a unique encoded code. Then, at inference time, a highly
realistic representation of the given input is produced by either learning
or inferring the entire codebook. Our method produces general representations
for data, such as videos, shapes and images, outperforming previous methods.

Traditional methods of covariate-shift adaptation utilize unlabelled data for either determining importance weights or domain-invariant features. Then, a model is trained using only labelled data. We're examining a special instance of covariate shift that also enables learning from unlabelled data, effectively merging adaptation with semi-supervised learning techniques. By drawing on causality concepts, we propose a novel method that requires learning from both the causes and effects of a target variable. This leads to the development of a semi-generative model, $P(Y,X_E|X_C,\theta)$, which is shown to be resilient against domain shifts in causal features. Moreover, this model leverages unlabelled data to directly map causes to their respective effects. Experiment results conducted on artificial data show considerable improvements in classification performance compared to solely-supervised and importance-weighting approaches.

Despite its impressive task execution capabilities, the inner workings of deep learning systems remain shrouded in theoretical uncertainty. In our study, we establish a geometric model for deep learning architectures by identifying connections to pre-existing geometric frameworks in quantum computation and diffeomorphic template matching. Within this context, we map the geometric structures of convolutional neural networks, residual networks, recursive neural networks, recurrent neural networks, and the equilibrium propagation framework. Furthermore, this geometric framework enables us to explore the relationships between geometric structures and the performance of different neural networks, thereby guiding the design of deep learning architectures at an algorithmic level.

We consider the field extension $\mathbb{Q}(\sqrt[3]{d},\zeta_3)/\mathbb{Q}(\zeta_3)$ where $\zeta_3$ is a primitive cube root of unity and $d$ is a positive cube-free integer. Our work examines the behavior of the chain of lattice minima in the cubic field $\mathbb{Q}(\sqrt[3]{d})$ arising from the prime factorization of $d$ in relation to generators of ambiguous principal ideals. Specifically, we investigate the occurrence of generators of such ideals among the lattice minima and explain their impact on the principal factorization type of the cubic field and its associated field extension when applying Voronoi's algorithm.

A research framework is introduced to uncover and analyze decision-making processes from deep neural network classifiers in jet substructure tagging techniques. This analysis tool allows researchers to identify key input variables, assess their relevance, and track information flow throughout the network. Utilizing this framework, the researchers scrutinized a renowned neural network classifier, identifying its variables and propagation of relevance to understand its underlying decision-making mechanisms. This analysis revealed that the classifier leverages jet constituents for accurate identification, but due to the non-linearity of the network, individual variables' contributions are obscure. This tool may be applied to various particle physics tagging methods and potentially other deep learning models.

For every positive integer r, a specific kind of Stirling number is used to count how many ways a set can be divided into a specified number of non-empty subsets, where each subset contains at least r elements. We're introducing a variation of these Stirling numbers, which represents their extreme forms, reducing to well-known cases when r equals one. This paper seeks to establish formulas linking these variations together.

Eighty sets of layer groups were examined, each consisting of four types: ordinary and double, as well as gray and double gray. Layer group properties allowed for the efficient computation of relevant physical characteristics using symbolic methods, thanks to code such as POLSym. This involved an initial step of categorizing irreducible domains based on their action within the Brillouin zone and the topology of the torus. Additionally, band representations stemming from site symmetry were broken down into irreducible components. This theoretical framework was then applied to classify ferromagnetic domains within ferroic compounds, such as Bi$_4$Fe$_3$O$_{12}$(NO$_3$)$_2$ and Bi$_4$Fe$_3$O$_{12}$Cl$_2$.

Momentum operators are explored in the context of intrinsically curved manifolds. It's established that for Killing vector fields representing these momentum operators, the manifolds are either flat or belong to specific categories: those with a compact structure and a constant sectional curvature of positive value, occurring in dimensions of 1, 3, or 7. Specific forms for these momentum operators and their associated Casimir element are studied, particularly for the three-dimensional sphere S^3. Furthermore, it is demonstrated that the Lie algebra structure constants for S^3 relate proportionally to 2R, where R represents the radius of the sphere.

A sign problem encountered in Monte Carlo simulations beyond half-filling can be mitigated by transforming the integration path. However, this requires intricate knowledge of the original path's characteristics. Our novel approach leverages a complex-valued neural network to learn the necessary transformation, ultimately enabling the successful application of the continuous-time Quantum Monte Carlo algorithm to a challenging Fermi sea scenario and the half-filled Hubbard model on an arbitrary lattice.

In a composite Higgs model, where $SU(6)/Sp(6)$ is used with three Flavon-Higgs bosons, we have found that a mild imbalance in their masses can naturally generate a sufficient anisotropy in the Yukawa coupling matrix for heavy fermions to explain the observed differences in their decay widths of $B$ mesons. This anomaly can be observed in the ratio of decay widths $\frac{f_{B_s}^{(CFT)}}{f_{B_d}^{(CFT)}}<1.1$. Furthermore, in a specific numerical example with heavy fermions' masses in a particular ratio, we have determined that the resulting anisotropy in the Yukawa matrix leads to significant deviations in several $B$ meson decay width ratios as predicted by the Flavon-Higgs boson scenario.

The use of Virtual-Physical Perceptual Manipulations, like redirected walking and haptics, extends VR interaction beyond conventional physical limitations by exploiting the boundaries of human perception, subtly guiding users' movements to enhance interactivity. This research examines the dangers of VPPM exploitation, beginning with a conceptual framework that confirms their existence and then applying speculative design to identify and mitigate threats. Through practical examples, we demonstrate how current VPPM practices can inadvertently create vulnerabilities that may lead to physical harm. This study seeks to highlight the potential consequences of VPPM applications and dissemination as they stand today.

To assess various approaches to expanding language coverage, we integrate German and Korean into BigScience's large-scale, 1.3 billion parameter multilingual language model, initially trained on 13 languages. Our study focuses on key factors influencing model adaptability for new languages and weighs the computational expense against potential performance gains.

Recent high-resolution observations using VLA and ALMA have uncovered numerous binary systems populating the field and young open clusters. This study seeks to examine the formation process of binary systems resulting from the spontaneous splitting of rotating parent cores of varying total mass. Our research utilized high-resolution calculations of the collapse of rotating parent cores with masses of one solar mass and three solar masses using a computational approach. What we found can be summarized as follows. When a binary system emerges from a core mass of one solar mass, its components have masses ranging from approximately 0.07 to 0.25 solar masses, with a mass ratio as low as 1.13. Both binary components form from the same parent core, with one mass function exhibiting a slope similar to that of the field stars, indicating a complete formation. Our results contradict the hypothesis suggesting binary components must originate from distinct molecular clouds. Increasing the core mass to three solar masses results in binary components with masses ranging from approximately 0.15 to 0.60 solar masses, including a low-mass satellite. Our findings are consistent with data from the field and young open clusters, including the data pointing to a binary mass function that slopes at a gentler angle. Our work may imply the existence of "binary-rich" protostellar cores, with a binary system potentially forming in every such core, as well as "binary-poor" cores, with no binary system forming.

This research introduces the m-arcsinh Kernel ('m-ar-K') Fast Independent Component Analysis ('FastICA') approach ('m-ar-K-FastICA') for feature extraction, combining the benefits of Kernel methods and FastICA. The novel approach leverages the kernel trick to transform data into a higher-dimensional space, where it can be analyzed using FastICA. Experimental outcomes using synthetic and real-world datasets demonstrate that m-ar-K-FastICA surpasses FastICA and related methods in accuracy, particularly for datasets containing nonlinear data patterns. Furthermore, m-ar-K-FastICA outperforms other comparison methods in relevant benchmark datasets.

This paper builds on existing research linking finite model theory to algebraic and propositional proof systems. It's proven that CPT-distinguishing formulas can be mapped to a specific class of algebraic proofs called VP, but with a limitation - this mapping only works for formulas that exhibit a particular property. Furthermore, the results show that CPT-distinguishing formulas which can be related to VP are constrained by a particular threshold on the amount of 'X-subsets' they use. In relation to NTP$_2$, the research finds that CPT-distinguishing formulas are restricted by the amount of 'X-subsets' they include. In the context of TLC, the study discovers that CPT-distinguishing formulas are restricted by both the amount of 'X-subsets' and 'Y-subsets' they use. In a broader sense, the research identifies that the capacity to distinguish graphs in a particular system is restricted by the complexity of the system's neighbourhood function. Additionally, the results suggest that the problem of determining whether a given graph can be distinguished in a particular system is likely to be NP-complete.

A subring collection in a ring $R$, that is associative, commutative nor unital, is defined as proper subrings set-theoretic union equating $R$. If such a collection exists, the ring covering number $\sigma(R)$ in $R$ is determined by the cardinality of a minimal collection, and a ring is $\sigma$ elementary when $\sigma(R) < \sigma(R/I)$ for any ideal of $R$, given it is non-zero, two sided and in $R$. The given text describes the discovery of first ring $\sigma$ elementary instances which possess non-trivial Jacobson radical $J$  and a ring that is non commutative in $R/J$, while determining ring covering numbers in $R$.

Social media platforms host an immense volume of user-generated content, encompassing a broad array of opinions on society, politics, and culture. This abundance of expressive content, although diverse, remains inaccessible to traditional information retrieval techniques due to their deficiency in dealing with unstructured, unverified claims. In response, we develop an innovative approach that combines neural language models with the inherent structure of online discourse, namely the hierarchical distribution of opinions across social media threads. By integrating this underlying structure into the retrieval process, we demonstrate substantial improvements over existing methods, showcasing that social media discussions are characterized by distinct thematic evolution patterns, which can be accurately identified through hierarchical topic modeling. Our findings serve as a foundation for developing new, structurally informed methods of information retrieval that can effectively navigate and make sense of the vast landscape of social media discourse.

Identifying trending social media events in real-time across various geographical locations is crucial, particularly for anticipating incidents such as accidents, protests, or breaking news. The dynamic nature of social media data poses challenges to traditional approaches, including ambiguous event timelines and spaces. An innovative solution is presented that leverages algorithms and statistical analysis to accurately determine event timelines and geographical areas from social media posts tagged with dates and locations, as well as to accurately rank events in terms of their popularity. The proposed method incorporates an adaptive filtering technique that filters out duplicate or fake events and accommodates variations in user-generated spatial and temporal data. Experimental results using real-world data on Australian social media reveal the proposed solution's ability to accurately detect and prioritize significant events across the country's entire geographical area.

New, high-precision data from the cosmic microwave background lensing measurements and tomographic galaxy surveys in the upcoming years will enable precise cross-correlation analysis in multiple $l$-bins. The conventional technique for analyzing the cross-correlation of lensing and galaxy data in multiple $l$-bins is quite time-consuming on large datasets. We have developed an efficient, fast covariance estimator specifically for analyzing the cross-correlation of lensing and galaxy data in multiple $l$-bins, which significantly reduces computational requirements by about two orders of magnitude. We compared the performance of our new estimator with the conventional technique on simulated data and found that our new estimator produces similar results. Our new estimator uses a fast and accurate estimator to calculate the lensing power spectrum, treats each $l$-bin independently, and includes galaxies in the calculation of the power spectrum, including those that span multiple $l$-bins. We also found that accounting for the effects of galaxy biasing and noise is crucial in achieving the best results.

By integrating Bayesian learning into adversarial training of deep neural networks, we developed a rigorous framework for training certifiable Bayesian Neural Networks. This approach combines constraint relaxation and modified cross-entropy loss to achieve robustness and learn a credible posterior distribution over class labels. We evaluated the method on various datasets, demonstrating its advantages in achieving improved robust accuracy and distribution tightness compared to previous techniques. This work has been accepted for a poster presentation at ICLR 2021.

The COVID-19 pandemic spread globally in early 2020 and caused severe consequences in China, also exacerbating public health anxiety fueled by rampant online rumors. To address this pressing issue, we examined the dynamics of rumor propagation and proposed a method to measure the impact of a rumor by tracking the speed of its new adopters. Utilizing search frequency as a proxy for this metric, we identified the peak and attenuation coefficients which conform to an exponential distribution. Subsequently, we developed and evaluated machine learning models, discovering that decision trees effectively forecast the peak coefficient and linear regression accurately predicts the attenuation coefficient. Our analysis indicated that certain precursor characteristics are crucial for predicting a rumor's peak influence, whereas location and entity information are more significant in determining its attenuation. Intriguingly, features indicating a rumor's harm or uncertainty actually contribute to its dissemination while features implying a rumor's non-harm or uncertainty actually predict its decline. Furthermore, pre-existing social connections among individuals were found to be irrelevant to the forecasting of a rumor's influence.

This study investigates the impact of hyperspectral pixel dimensionality reduction on classification tasks. Five methods (PCA, KPCA, ICA, AE, and DAE) are utilized to compress high-dimensional pixels down to 301 dimensions. The resulting pixels are used for classification, allowing a comprehensive assessment of each method's effectiveness based on classification accuracy, compression rates, and reconstruction errors. Our research employed three diverse hyperspectral image datasets (urban, suburban, and forest landscapes), gathered by the Remote Sensing and Spatial Ecosystem Modeling lab at the University of Toronto. Our analysis reveals that PCA, KPCA, and ICA methods preserve pixel signals well but show decreased classification performance beyond 90% compression rates. In contrast, AE and DAE achieve better results at 95% compression but see their performance deteriorate as the compression rate approaches 97%. Ultimately, our findings highlight the importance of considering both compression methods and rates when crafting an effective hyperspectral pixel classification workflow.

Neural networks are highly effective feature extractors but they pose significant challenges due to their large size. Understanding the parameters within various layers is complicated, resulting in the networks often being referred to as 'black boxes.' In contrast, simpler models are more interpretable but they are also much harder to find. Identifying and utilizing a sparse network that can be trained to replicate the same results is a viable option to improve network interpretability. According to the lottery ticket hypothesis, even large, dense neural networks harbor a smaller sparse sub-network that can be trained independently to achieve the same accuracy in the original task. Our objective is to explore the existence of this trainable sub-network in the realm of natural language processing by examining various methods of network pruning that have been previously proposed.

A novel prediction method, referred to as ProCS, enables rapid calculation of crucial chemical shift indicators in proteins, thereby determining the spatial arrangements of proteins. ProCS is calibrated with the results of high-level quantum mechanical calculations, producing remarkably precise predictions for the amide proton chemical shifts in proteins. Studies using ProCS have revealed its potential to refine protein structures, assess the accuracy of predicted structures, and monitor changes within proteins. ProCS is an advanced tool that integrates quantum mechanical principles with the determination of protein spatial arrangements, offering enhanced accuracy in comparison to earlier versions. ProCS is now available online in the form of a publicly-accessible web server.

The choice of loss function for a neural network is widely regarded as a key decision with far-reaching implications, given the numerous loss functions developed to date, making it crucial to carefully select one. Despite its significance, research on the topic often omits explicit justification for loss function selection. We contend that this lack of justification reflects an untested assumption prevalent within the deep learning community. In this research, we investigate how loss function impacts performance in a supervised classification context. Our findings reveal that certain, previously underappreciated loss functions, including the KL divergence, can yield superior outcomes compared to established methods, underscoring the need to view loss function choice as a parameter amenable to optimization, rather than a fixed constant.

Describing the behaviors of complex systems comprised of strongly interacting elements requires concise expressions for their internal relationships. Ensuring the stability of these systems is the primary focus. Parquet theory is capable of achieving a level of self-consistency that encompasses all strictly pair-based interactions among elements. Grounded in a perturbative framework, the theory is comprised of a series of nonlinear integral equations that describe scattering events at all levels of the system. However, the absence of a comprehensive theoretical framework for obtaining a convergent expansion series presents a significant challenge. In this study, we present an innovative approach to parquet theory, predicated on a new integral equation that governs the overall system behavior. This approach is rooted in a broader theoretical framework known as $N$-point theory. By developing a new integral equation, we demonstrate an improved convergence of the parquet theory expansion series, effectively addressing one of the field's longstanding hurdles. Furthermore, we show that this improved approach is applicable to a wide range of systems, including those defined by an Hamiltonian. Specifically, we applied this methodology to a system of interacting bosons and fermions, achieving a breakthrough by deriving a fully Hamiltonian-based parquet theory for any element type. In particular, we were able to obtain a precise expression for the element's response function, enabling a profound understanding of system behavior at its fundamental level.

The process of exciton condensation leads to the spontaneous creation of electron-hole pairs and triggers a phase transition in a semimetal that forms an excitonic insulator by creating a gap at the Fermi surface. This theoretical concept has been around for decades, but current approaches only offer approximate solutions; therefore, a reliable prediction tool remains to be developed. To address this issue, researchers have developed a new method based on a precise computational approach and tested it on the material TiSe2, which is known to undergo an exciton condensation-induced phase transition. By modeling the material using a simplified approach that only includes the most important wavefunctions, the study found that the obtained results, which include the created gap at the Fermi surface and the characteristics of the new phase, aligned with experimental observations, which supports the theoretical framework of the phase transition. Furthermore, the precise nature of the computational approach also enabled researchers to analyze the material's properties using a more rigorous statistical method, which provided additional insights into the material's behavior.

In the US, various safety organizations have adopted text-based systems for processing community members' incident reports, which necessitated a closer look at interactions between community members and dispatchers through these platforms. To investigate, researchers analyzed the system logs of LiveSafe, a community safety tool, combining quantitative and qualitative methods to identify patterns in the conversational flow. By developing a data framework that captured common incident-related information, researchers discovered dispatchers requested specific details from users, which varied based on incident types. Furthermore, emotion analysis and regression testing revealed disparities in the emotional support provided by dispatchers across different organizations and incident categories. Notably, dispatchers who showed emotional support received higher response rates and faster responses from users. These results have provided significant knowledge to practitioners and system designers, inspiring the development of AI-powered tools to enhance human service quality.

To analyze the impact of external magnetization on doped Bi$_2$Se$_3$ with spin-triplet nematic superconductivity, we computationally investigate magnetic susceptibility in nematic and chiral superconducting states using the Ginzburg-Landau formalism near its critical temperature. A key observation in this analysis is that the superconducting order parameter shows a non-trivial response to the transverse component of an applied magnetic field, which can result in a paramagnetic response. Moreover, the topology of the Fermi surface exerts a substantial influence on magnetic susceptibility, with a specific Lifshitz transition inducing a transition from the nematic to the chiral phase and leading to the divergence of magnetic susceptibility at this transition point. Notably, the interplay between electron-electron interaction and competing phases of superconductivity is investigated, with results showing that the driving force behind a transition from the nematic to the chiral phase can be the presence of electron-electron interaction in the immediate vicinity of the transition. A comparison with existing experimental data is also presented in this analysis.

Label-efficient active learning algorithms query specific, representative samples to be annotated by a human. Present techniques either utilize a model's uncertainty or rely on diversity measures, such as clustering or reconstruction, to choose unlabeled examples. However, model uncertainty-based methods are susceptible to outliers and diversity-based methods may overlook key information. To address this, we introduce a semi-supervised active learning approach that simultaneously considers both uncertainty and diversity in a minimax framework. Our method incorporates a network that minimizes entropy and an entropy-maximizing classifier, while a discriminator is trained to distinguish labeled and unlabeled data. We then select the samples with the highest entropy that the discriminator identifies as unlabeled for human annotation. Experimental evaluation on image classification and semantic segmentation datasets demonstrates superior performance compared to state-of-the-art methods.

To study how music changed over time from the year 1960 to 2010, we measured the
variety of songs in the Million Song Dataset using several elements, including
melodic quality, texture, volume, and rhythmic patterns. By analyzing the popular
hits listed on the Billboard Hot 100 and randomly selected songs, we found that
most hit songs tend to be musically straightforward with characteristics close to
the average. This discovery aligns with the theory that songs with moderate levels of
variety tend to be most appealing to the average listener. Furthermore, our
research revealed significant changes in song composition over the past fifty years,
showing significant decreases in texture and dynamic range but steady increases in
 rhythmic complexity. This findings confirm the observations of previous music
experts while also providing further support.

A novel category of stochastic processes that incorporate reinforcement involves sequences of random groupings denoted as $\{\mathcal{A}_t\}_{t=1}^{\infty}$, where each $\mathcal{A}_t$ is a random selection of distinct objects from a set $\mathcal{S}_T$ typically increasing in size $T$. The fundamental probability measure that a particular object $s$ is included in $\mathcal{A}_t$ at time $t$ is referred to as the inclusion probability distribution, function, or model, depending on the object's characteristics and the point in time $t$. The inclusion probability that an object $s$ is part of $\mathcal{A}_t$ at time $t$ is denoted as $\mathbb{P}_t(s\in\mathcal{A}_t)$. The objects within each $\mathcal{A}_t$ are fully independent from those in previous groups $\mathcal{A}_u$ for $u<t$. The investigation into the inclusion probability that an object appears across multiple groups $\mathmathcal{A}_t$ for $1\leq t\leq T$ at time $t$ is known as the long-term multiple-entry reinforcement problem in stochastic processes. Prawitz identified a key feature of Gentzen's intuitionistic natural deduction as the inversion principle, typically paired in proof-theoretic literature with the recovery principle. This paper proposes an alternative, that the recovery principle can be replaced with a generalized form of the cut-elimination theorem, dubbed the harmony condition. A specific formulation of this condition is achieved through the application of a specific pigeonhole principle in the context of the harmonic extension of the structured natural deduction framework, developed by Baudart and Bostedahl.

A prominent paradigm in reward learning utilizes human feedback via comparative evaluations, but their broader adoption is hindered by the expense and labor intensity of these comparisons. To overcome this limitation, we propose grouping multiple comparisons together and allowing human labelers to mark sub-regions of a condensed state space representation, thereby efficiently leveraging human time. Through data visualization techniques, we create an interactive interface for users to label these regions, thereby effectively enhancing the learning agents' performance, even when human labeling time remains constant, across basic Mujoco tasks.

We show that a topological space's Smyth powerspace is core-compact if and only if the original space has local compactness. Consequently, this implies the Smyth powerspace does not uniformly preserve core-compact properties.

We're investigating singular vorticities in ideal two-dimensional fluids with specific properties derived from point vortices and vortex sheets. These characteristics are embodied in "pointed vortex loops," allowing us to concentrate on their corresponding orbits under area-preserving diffeomorphisms on the 2D real plane. The results show that a specific subgroup within these diffeomorphisms preserves the shape of the vortex loop itself, indicating the configuration space is comprised of loops confining a fixed area regardless of the vorticity distribution and any connected points.

The Average Treatment Effect (ATE) is a causal parameter that can be estimated in two steps, initially modeling treatment and outcome variables, then incorporating prediction errors into weighted estimators. Previous methods have addressed non-normal distributions of predictions, but this paper proposes a new normalized augmented inverse probability weighting (NAIPW) estimator applicable to both Gaussian and non-Gaussian distributions. The proposed NAIPW performs better in high-dimensional scenarios and achieves asymptotic efficiency equivalent to the efficient naive IPW estimator under specific conditions. The method is further demonstrated on simulated data and real-world applications, revealing substantial improvements in bias and root mean squared error compared to traditional IPW estimation.

The role of $\tau$ is taking center stage in the current research into lepton flavor universality violations in B-physics, warranting greater theoretical attention in the coming years. Enhanced data samples from Belle-II, as well as LHCb, ATLAS, and CMS, will be crucial in further investigating the topic. Additionally, insights from $\tau$ decays into its spin will be particularly beneficial. If experimental findings of new physics prevail, it is anticipated that new CP-odd phases will be necessary to align B-meson form factors, while CP-even new strong interactions or leptoquarks could account for observed discrepancies in $R_K$. If no new physics is detected, enhanced precision on the $\tau$ lepton itself will be the primary outcome, offering opportunities to update SM forecasts with data from $\tau$ decays into 1 gamma and electron and muon pairs.

A tabletop-sized rotating annulus setup has been extensively studied to mimic the general circulation of mid-latitude atmospheric circulation. The device effectively replicates two crucial factors contributing to cyclogenesis, namely the influence of rotation and temperature variations, in a simple yet comprehensive arrangement. The laboratory model enables researchers to control and analyze the formation of baroclinic waves through adjustments in temperature gradients and rotational rates, thereby creating distinctive wave patterns at the free surface of the rotating liquid. These experiments were conducted alongside numerical simulations by five groups from the MetStr\"om collaboration, utilizing different methods and approaches to validate their results. The obtained wave patterns were then analyzed, compared, and documented to establish benchmarks for further evaluation in upcoming assessment cycles focused on modeling baroclinic wave development and dynamics.

A typical strategy for modelling extreme events involves considering occurrences beyond a high threshold as events of a non-homogeneous Poisson process. While this method has the advantage of using threshold-independent extreme value parameters, it comes with the challenge of parameter interdependence, making estimation more complicated. We introduce a novel approach that converts the standard estimation problem into a simpler one under a specific transformation. As a result, this new approach enables the efficient application of global optimisation techniques and easy comparison of models. Furthermore, our framework accommodates various model types, including those based on spatial, temporal, and temporal-by-spatial non-homogeneities. Ultimately, this study aims to provide a framework for modelling extreme events and investigating their spatial and temporal patterns.

In the field of offline reinforcement learning, we focus on adversarial robustness, a critical consideration in RL that deals with the challenge of learning a nearly optimal policy when a fraction of data in the training dataset has been compromised by an adversary. Our study begins by examining a worst-case scenario involving the linear Markov decision process and finding that even with the adversary only modifying the reward in each data tuple, a certain threshold of optimality gap cannot be avoided. Conversely, in contrast to robust supervised learning, which has seen significant breakthroughs with little dimension-related impact and similar lower bounds for the online RL with data corruption. Moreover, we introduce robust variants of Least-Square Value Iteration that are applicable both when data coverage is complete and when it is incomplete. These robust LSVO variants show promising performance, but in instances of data incompleteness, we require prior knowledge of epsilon for the bonus of pessimism to function. Unexpectedly, we discovered that the adaptability to the value of epsilon when its value is not previously known is impossible, which highlights that the problem of offline robust RL is even more challenging.

This study demonstrates a logarithmic convexity linked to observability at a specific point in time for a one-dimensional heat equation under dynamic boundary conditions, leading to impulse approximate controllability in similar scenarios with dynamic boundaries. Additionally, we provide a detailed estimate for the cost of impulse control. Our research includes a step-by-step procedure for finding the impulsive control of minimal L^2-norm and supports these findings with numerical tests to verify the efficiency of the developed algorithm.

A consensus has not been established on the definition and optimal detection methods for out-of-distribution examples despite general agreement on their importance. We identified distinct behaviors of two major detection methods - model calibration and density estimation - in response to background and semantic shifts in data, which were found across various language understanding datasets. In our evaluation, density estimation outperformed model calibration in background shift scenarios and exhibited more consistent performance across different settings of interest. Nonetheless, both approaches demonstrated an inability to detect out-of-distribution examples with high semantic similarity to in-distribution data. Our findings suggest that current methods are insufficient for detecting truly out-of-distribution data and that more research is required to develop effective solutions for such challenging examples.

In recent years, various artificial molecular motors utilizing electric currents have been explored, and like Brownian machines, they generate directional rotation from random tunneling events. Despite the abundance of research on these systems, there has not been a comprehensive theoretical model available until now. We have developed a realistic model that describes the dynamics of these machines and is in agreement with experimental findings. This new model provides a valuable tool for designing and optimizing molecular motors and investigating their behavior.

Building on a 2014 framework, researchers introduced various interpretations of transducer behavior, some differing significantly from traditional understandings. In this study, further insights into close approximations between two-way and one-way transducer models were gained. Specifically, we demonstrate the possibility of determining whether a non-deterministic two-way word transducer can be transformed into an equivalent one-way model, with a limit to how complex this transformation can be. Notably, this outcome contradicts traditional transducer equivalences, which were shown to be indeterminable in certain scenarios.

In this study, we investigate the concept of general convolution by considering the set of all possible $n$-dimensional vectors from a finite domain $D$, where the elements of these vectors can take on values from $D$. A specific operation, denoted as $\oplus_f$, is defined as the application of function $f$ to pairs of elements from $D$ applied element-wise. This enables us to define a new convolution, known as the $f$-Convolution, for two given functions $g$ and $h$, each mapping $n$-dimensional vectors from $D$ to integers between $-M$ and $M$. By applying $\oplus_f$ to pairs of $n$-dimensional vectors $x$ and $y$, and then evaluating the applied function $h$, we can calculate the $f$-Convolution, or "convolution product," of $g(x)$ and $h(y)$. This leads us to formulate two distinct problems: the Computation Problem, which involves computing $g(x)\oplus_f h(y)$, and the Generalized Problem, which adds the requirement that we also compute $h(x)\oplus_f g(y)$. We prove that these problems can be solved more efficiently than through brute force for certain types of functions, particularly those that are "monotone," which means their output value increases or remains the same when individual input elements increase. The discovery of T-Dwarf GJ 229B in 1995 offered initial insight into its composition, yet a detailed analysis with current spectroscopic methods has been lacking, especially concerning its atmospheric features, which display unusual properties and contradict earlier estimates of the dwarf's mass and orbit, requiring further examination due to their implications for intermediate population object formation processes. With a distance of tens of astronomical units from its host star, GJ 229B exists near the boundary between the planetary and stellar domains, offering an opportunity for its atmospheric analysis to shed light on formation mechanisms. By utilizing the open-source APOLLO code for a thorough spectral analysis across 0.5-5.1 ${\rm \mu m}$, we derived a precise mass estimate of $41.6\pm3.3\, M_J$ and an accurate temperature assessment of $869_{-7}^{+5}$ K that corresponds with evolutionary models, indicating the system to be older than 1 billion years, and also identified high CO molecular abundance replicating earlier observations, which provide implications for this object's formation and evolution, further contributing to the knowledge of analyzing brown dwarfs and planets through new-generation telescopes.

To search for the potential existence of the unique $0^{--}$ state, we created a systematic approach to designing tetraquark operators. In the process, we found that $0^{+-}$ tetraquark operators without derivatives are not possible. Due to the distinct Lorentz structure of the $0^{--}$ currents, it is prevented from incorporating corrections from four-quark terms into its spectral density, leading the gluon condensate to become the primary factor influencing the spectral density as power correction within the context of the finite energy sum rule. Our results from the sum rule analysis with the use of seven designed interpolating currents, however, indicate the lack of evidence to support a resonant signal related to the exotic $0^{--}$ state, leading us to conclude its absence below 2 GeV.

A crucial goal of the LHCb experiment is to establish the $C\!P$-violating phase $\phi_{s}$ and decay width difference $\Delta\Gamma_{s}$ caused by $\bar{b}\to\bar{c}c\bar{s}$ decays. The precise prediction of $\phi_{s}$ within the Standard Model makes it a favorable means for detecting signs of new physics. The experiment's $\phi_{s}$ and $\Delta\Gamma_{s}$ measurements are discussed in detail, encompassing the 2011-2012 data set of 3.0~fb$^{-1}$. Future analyses are expected to contribute significantly through the incorporation of additional results derived from decay modes with reduced branching fractions.

Airborne transmission risk in confined environments like buses is intricately affected by the interplay between turbulent airflow, respiration processes, coughing, and sneezing, as well as various ventilation methods, temperature-driven buoyancy effects, and surface deposition of aerosols. To better understand and quantify this complex dynamic, we used numerical models of unsteady airflow to analyze and visualize virus-laden aerosol transport. In comparing our detailed model to existing studies of a similar scenario, we found notable discrepancies between predicted outcomes and earlier reports. This mismatch highlights the potential benefits of detailed modeling in predicting transmission risk, particularly when the underlying assumptions of simpler models prove inaccurate.

This study has conducted large-scale shell-model computations for $\beta$-decay attributes. Researchers at ILL, Grenoble, recently performed $\beta$-delayed $\gamma$-ray spectroscopy to investigate $\beta$-decay properties related to the transition of $^{137}$Te ($7/2^-$) to $^{137}$I with various final $J$-values. We conducted a comprehensive shell-model analysis of nuclear properties and compared our results to experimental findings. We then reported our computed $\beta$-decay attributes, such as the $\log ft$ values and the mean shape factors. Our study marks the first theoretical calculation for $\log ft$ values in conjunction with these novel experimental data. Additionally, we also calculated the $\log ft$ results for $^{135}$Te ($7/2^-$) decaying into $^{135}$I with different $J$-values.

Double-sided auctions are commonly used in financial markets to facilitate matching of demand and supply. Our work builds on prior research, which mainly focused on handling a single quantity of trade requests. To expand this knowledge, we developed methods to support multiple quantity trade requests and established fully formalized matching algorithms for double-sided auctions. These algorithms come with rigorous correctness proofs. Additionally, we formulated new theorems for verifying the uniqueness of an exchange's output, allowing for automatic detection of potential program violations. To ensure the accuracy of our work, all the mathematical proofs were conducted using the Coq proof assistant.

We utilized heavy quark effective theory to investigate the $F$-wave bottom mesons, applying both theoretical and experimental data to calculate the mass of these mesons. Additionally, by examining the decay widths of bottom mesons, we derived upper limits on their corresponding coupling values. Our research further included constructing Regge trajectories in the planes of angular momentum (J) and squared mass (M^2), yielding predictions that align neatly with Regge theory lines. These outcomes may hold significant implications for future experimental research on this topic.

Michal Szabados initially proposed a theory in his doctoral dissertation. In this current paper, the proposed conjecture is examined by the authors, specifically a Ph.D. hypothesis by Michal Szabados. Initially, the researchers demonstrate that an evaluation could be narrowed down to a periodic structure, defined over a specific and limited character set. It is further established that Szabados's conjecture is true for a considerable class of non-regular patterns. This includes all low-convex patterns of relatively simple complexity.

In modern research on data-driven systems, a primary focus lies on overcoming challenges presented by high-dimensional complexities, hidden system dynamics, and the presence of nonlinearity.  The dynamic mode decomposition technique has proven valuable in creating models from large data sets, yet the effectiveness of these models can be hindered by inaccurate assumptions regarding the linearity of the system and the quality of the snapshot alignment.  Furthermore, the process of identifying a linear model that minimally deviates from the nonlinearity of the system poses an intricate optimization problem.  This paper introduces a new method called Linear and Nonlinear Displacement Optimization (LANDO), which utilizes kernel methods to develop a data-driven approach for accurately mapping the dynamics of a system while accounting for nonlinear transformations and the potential existence of multiple distinct phases within the system's dynamics.  The effectiveness of the LANDO method is demonstrated through its application on two complex systems: a case study involving a numerically simulated system with multiple phases and a numerically simulated system with significant nonlinear components.

The timeless appeal of chess persists, with its strategic intricacies still captivating players across the globe, from casual enthusiasts to world-class champions. Despite substantial advancements in artificial intelligence, the intricate complexities of chess openings have long defied comprehensive analysis. Our research delves into the uncharted world of chess openings, leveraging data from the largest online chess community, over 300 million recorded games, to uncover new insights. By employing a sophisticated multi-layer network model, we're able to map the global preferences of chess players, visualize opening sequences, and quantify the complexity and similarity of chess openings in distinct eras. Our innovative approach combines online community data with a substantial review of existing literature, yielding valuable contributions to the field of complex system study.

This research explores the observational characteristics of millisecond pulsars in terms of their magnetic fields, rotational periods, and masses. Our analysis is grounded in the concept of accretion-induced collapse of white dwarfs within binary star systems, enabling a more nuanced comprehension of millisecond pulsar demographics. Moreover, our findings underscore the significant evolutionary linkage between neutron stars and white dwarfs within stellar binary systems, particularly through the process of accretion-induced collapse.

A method to derive constants of motion beyond local bounds for ODE-based Lagrangian systems is outlined, including a practical example that illustrates its utility for dissipative mechanical systems and its implications on solution existence and behavior under specific assumptions. The framework is further extended to cover Euler-Lagrange equations with order greater than two, yielding new first integrals for particular models, such as the Pais-Uhlenbeck oscillator, paving the way for potential applications in Euler-Lagrange partial differential equations in the future.

Developing free online collections of 3D shapes has driven research in 3D retrieval. Debates surrounding the optimal input method for retrieval and the ultimate application have been ongoing. In this research, we present an alternative approach by focusing on using 3D sketches as input and envisioning a virtual reality (VR) environment for retrieval. We aim to allow users to freely access 3D models through air-drawn sketches in a VR setting. As an initial step, our study contributes four aspects: implementing a tool to collect and retrieve 3D sketches in VR, gathering the first dataset of $167$ sketches in two categories from ModelNet, developing a novel approach to generate synthetic human-like sketches, and evaluating the performance of different approaches. We observed that in the context of sketch-based retrieval, volumetric point-based 3D models perform better than surface-based models. We propose two methods that outperformed traditional methods and achieved 74% and 65% accuracy in retrieving synthetic and real sketches, respectively. Additionally, we observed the potential of leveraging early fusion in 3D sketching and retrieval, which resulted in a 5% improvement in retrieval accuracy. We will present two more approaches at the conference, which utilize data augmentation and hierarchical feature matching to enhance sketch-based retrieval.

HD80606b, a planet that passes directly in front of its host star, undergoes a significant 1000-fold increase in the heat it receives due to its highly eccentric 111-day orbit. As the planet rapidly moves close to its star, its surface temperature jumps dramatically from 400K to over 1400K in a matter of hours during its closest approach. Observations using the James Webb Space Telescope will soon take advantage of this planet's extraordinary environment to study various aspects of its atmosphere. Accurate information about HD80606b's orbit is crucial to making the most out of these observations. Researchers have conducted in-depth analyses of the planet's transits on February 7, 2020, and December 7-8, 2021, in collaboration with the TESS spacecraft and a global network of small telescopes. Additionally, they obtained new velocity measurements which were combined with the transit data, ultimately leading to a more precise estimate of the planet's orbital path. As a result, the margin of error for predicting transit and eclipse events around HD80606b has been reduced to a matter of minutes. This new level of accuracy may allow researchers to detect subtle irregularities in the planet's orbit when combined with upcoming observations using the James Webb Space Telescope.

In this investigation, we're looking at how a specific type of matter collapse, governed by a certain relationship between pressure and density, behaves according to the general theory of relativity. The effect of this relationship on the mass function is analyzed in terms of its consistency with the general relativity equations, and we find that when this relationship holds, it's usually difficult to get consistent solutions. The outcomes of this type of collapse are then explored, along with the effect of additional factors, such as pressure in a collapsing cloud. Since accurately modeling such a situation is hard due to lack of information about its initial state, we consider small changes in density instead. These small changes cause tiny fluctuations in pressure, which in turn affect the space where this matter lives. By studying these fluctuations numerically, we can understand how these small changes affect the space as well.

Using the Iyer-Wald formalism, we have developed a comprehensive method for determining corrections to the extremality bounds and entropy of Kerr-Newman black holes following any arbitrary perturbation. This method involves integrating an effective stress tensor and shows, under certain conditions, the correction is equivalent to the standard stress tensor, thereby illuminating the relationship between extremality corrections and energy conditions. Furthermore, we have demonstrated that to lower the mass of an extremal black hole in a canonical ensemble as stipulated by the weak gravity conjecture, the perturbation must breach the dominant energy condition. We have successfully applied this method to compute higher-order corrections to black holes in anti-de Sitter space and to Kerr black holes.

A key goal in reinforcement learning is to invert a target outcome distribution, which can be achieved using end-effect drives to implement goal-oriented motor learning, even without an explicit predictive model. End-effect models utilize a straightforward statistical representation of policy effects, which serve as a substitute for more computationally intensive predictive models. When combined with a reward structure, they form the foundation of a streamlined variational free energy minimization system. However, the primary challenge is balancing the upkeep of this simplified effect model with the policy's continuous updates. Interestingly, when the target distribution is uniform, our approach facilitates learning an efficient exploratory policy consistent with the principles of intrinsic curiosity. Moreover, when paired with an external reward, our method yields faster training times than traditional off-policy techniques.

A generalized three-dimensional Poincaré algebra has been developed that incorporates colour symmetry. This enhanced algebra can serve as a basis for modelling coloured Poincaré gravity and exploring generalised models of massive and massless free particles in three dimensions. Multiple generalised particle models have been presented, which distinguish themselves in terms of the coloured Poincaré orbits they describe. Our methodology provides a potential pathway to describing particles in non-abelian backgrounds and serves as a starting point for the worldline formulation of an associated quantum field theory.

We have devised three new parameterized algorithms for identifying whether a directed graph can be represented in an upward planar layout. Specifically, we've developed a fixed-parameter algorithm based on the number of source vertices, an XP algorithm based on the graph's treewidth, and a fixed-parameter algorithm based on the treedepth parameter. Our novel method combines parameterized techniques with SPQR tree-decompositions, extending previous tractability findings on series-parallel graphs, single-source graphs, and outerplanar graphs.

Image-based goal navigation is a difficult problem, requiring agents to navigate to visually identified objectives in unfamiliar environments.
Previous methods often employ diverse memory mechanisms to track navigation history but fail to account for the fraction of relevant information in their memories.
We propose the MemoNav framework, which incorporates multiple memory mechanisms and a novel objective function that prioritizes informative memories to guide navigation.
Experimental results demonstrate that MemoNav surpasses existing navigation methods utilizing various memory types and achieves this improvement by leveraging diverse memories and weightingly aggregating their fractions of relevant information.

To increase cellular capacity, operators initially implemented 4G LTE small cells (Femto Cells) eight years ago. The role of LTE small cells is now clear in addressing indoor coverage issues and will likely play a crucial part in future 5G and future generations of wireless communication systems. This paper summarizes my previous work on small cells, specifically on LTE and 5G NR, and discusses the ongoing and anticipated developments in this field, incorporating recent research findings. The aim is to provide insight into how small cells will be integrated into future wireless networks.

We've developed a comprehensive framework to model complex interactions between multiple entangled systems across various contexts by applying the multiplex network concept. In response to a thought-provoking question posed in a previous study, our framework enables the analysis of systems that become irreversibly linked, leading to a crucial insight into the essential threshold for system instability. To further generalize existing theories, our framework extends the application of dynamical systems to complex hypergraph systems, providing new avenues for exploration.

This study examines the operator growth phenomenon in Lie-symmetric systems by utilizing concepts from quantum information theory. We specifically analyze Krylov complexity, entanglement properties, and information capacity within SU(1,1) and SU(2) symmetric systems, leveraging two-mode coherent states as a primary tool. These coherent states enable us to explore operator growth patterns and entanglement structures in a systematic manner, ultimately verifying that certain fundamental features emerge across these systems in alignment with the universal operator growth hypothesis.

The atomic structure of the Hoyle state, a state consisting of highly clustered $\alpha$ particles at 7.65 MeV in $^{12}\mathrm{C}$, has been a topic of interest for a long time. The question of whether this system consists of three weakly-interacting $\alpha$ particles in the 0s orbital is crucial and can be answered by analyzing the decay paths of the Hoyle state. Our research presents the latest findings on the direct 3 $\alpha$ decay of the Hoyle state, which were gathered through ultra-low background measurements conducted using the TEXO experiment. Our data shows that 99.8% of the decays occur through a specific angular relationship, indicating a specific, aligned structure to the 0s orbital. Our results contradict existing theoretical predictions of the Hoyle state structure, rather suggesting a more compact, clustered structure.

Significant breakthroughs in understanding and computation of fracture instability have been achieved for 2D dynamic fracture. The essence of this advancement is the identification of intrinsic scales at crack tips - nonlinear elastic length and dissipation length scales - which are absent in classical fracture theory. Studies have shown that in hard materials under high velocities, an oscillatory instability emerges, while in softer materials, an intricate branching pattern often develops at the crack tip through a non-linear transition. In the intermediate regime, a striking "V"-shaped formation can occur, potentially leading to further splitting. The identification of these intrinsic scales has Breakdown in Soft Materials in 2D Dynamic Fracture.

In a general setting, we examine the properties of finite state channels equipped with feedback and state information, which becomes available to the encoder in a predictable sequence. This encompasses a broad range of channels, including memoryless channels with independent and identically distributed states (referred to as the Shannon strategy), channels with Markovian states that offer the ability to access past states (known as look-ahead access) and energy harvesting. The capacity of these channels with feedback is described in terms of the directed information between auxiliary variables and the channel outputs. Additionally, we propose two distinct methods for determining this capacity: a method involving the development of an infinite-horizon average-reward dynamic programming system and a method utilizing auxiliary directed graphs called Q-graphs. These methods are applied to various illustrative examples, with a particular example examining a channel with look-ahead access, for which we establish a closed-form lower bound on the capacity. Furthermore, our methods are shown to accurately calculate the capacity of well-studied channels, including unifilar channels such as the trapdoor, Ising and input-constrained erasure channels. Finally, we analyze a channel with a state dependent on the input in a random manner and derive a precise formula for the capacity of this channel with feedback in the scenario where the states are uniformly distributed.

A novel class of superconductors featuring antisymmetric spin-orbit coupling and placed within a Zeeman magnetic field may be used to create fault-tolerant quantum computations via topologically non-Abelian states. Employing a quantum Monte Carlo dynamical cluster approximation, we analyzed the effects of Rashba spin-orbit coupling and Zeeman field on superconductivity in a two-dimensional attractive Hubbard model with doping. Our findings reveal that Rashba coupling enhances s-wave superconductivity, overcoming Zeeman field-induced pair-breaking when present. Additionally, we demonstrate that Rashba coupling counteracts the spin imbalance caused by the Zeeman field through mixing, thus restoring superconductivity. Furthermore, we established that Rashba coupling's favorable impact on superconductivity originates from a spin-flip driven enhancement of the likelihood of a pair of electrons traveling in reverse time-states. Our analysis also predicts that under suitable Rashba coupling and Zeeman field conditions, the superconducting state exhibits topologically non-trivial characteristics, as confirmed through inspection of the interacting model's Fermi surface.

This study focuses on understanding and interpreting tables, requiring the ability to recognize their structure and compare cell information effectively. To address this challenge, we introduced a new dataset for SemEval 2020 Task 9: SEM-TAB-FACTS, aiming to enhance natural language processing capabilities by verifying factual information and locating supporting evidence within tabular data. The comprehensive dataset comprised 981 manually crafted tables and an automatically generated collection of 1980 tables, encompassing a total of 3210 assertions for evaluation purposes. The evaluation took place in July 2020, with participants submitting their findings and research on identifying and verifying table-based factual assertions and pinpointing supporting evidence in tabular data. This summary presents the dataset and evaluation results from SEM-TAB-FACTS, highlighting participants' performance and achievements in this area.

This analysis explores the essential role of complex numbers in Quantum Mechanics, delving into common justifications for complex formalism and offering additional perspectives to support its necessity. By examining these factors, we hope to clarify the underlying reasoning for employing complex numbers in Quantum mechanics.

A graph G is considered fully identifiable when a subset of its vertices R can pinpoint each vertex uniquely by determining their distance to every point in R. A sub-set of R that does this best with the fewest points is known as the minimum identifying set or "metric dimension" of the graph. Here we discuss the version of this property where the shortest distances between points are capped at some number k and call it beta_k of the graph.

These notes document my process of reviewing equations governing distant groundwater movement for a paper. By "distant," I'm referring to horizontal distances exceeding the thickness of the aquifer. They're based on assumptions discussed later on. These equations aren't an original contribution but rather a reference point for those working in applied mathematics interested in modeling groundwater flow.

This work has investigated the potential of integrating an ozone O3 and ultraviolet (UV) light system for effectively eliminating pollutants in flue gas emissions. A numerical model of a continuous stirred tank reactor (CSTR) was used to simulate and analyze the removal of sulfur dioxide SO2 through gas-phase oxidation. Various UV radiation models were considered, each representing the complex interaction between light and matter. The study examined the influence of numerous parameters, including radiation models, UV intensity, ozone O3 injection rates, temperature, and gas phase Sulfuric Acid Film Transfer Reactions. Different scenarios were explored using the global reaction mechanism for sulfur dioxide, including both homogeneous and heterogeneous reactions. The results showed that a combination of radical mapping and the direct kinetic model accurately represented the gas-phase reaction kinetics, whereas heterogeneous reactions were best simulated using the physical film model. The application of the physical film model revealed the significance of mass transfer in the overall reaction process.

As interest in neuromorphic computing grows, engineers face a key challenge in simulating the technology to evaluate and refine it. Testing neural network applications on simulated neuromorphic systems requires significant computational power, making it a crucial benchmark for evaluating different architecture designs. To speed up simulations, leveraging the multi-core capabilities of host systems is essential. This paper proposes a parallelized simulation environment based on SystemC for RISC-V multi-core platforms that incorporates multiple computing-in-memory accelerators for neuromorphic computing. The authors also investigate and demonstrate various simulation architectures for integrating these accelerators, comparing the efficiency gains against conventional sequential simulation approaches.

Deploying machine learning in practical scenarios can often present challenges, primarily stemming from uninterpretable models, questionable reliance on imperfect data, or offering a sole prediction outcome without considering various possibilities. This study attempts to rectify these issues by developing a novel framework based on decision trees, aiming to tackle reasoning and learning challenges in a systematic and transparent manner. Furthermore, the framework is designed to handle uncertainty-related concerns, learning difficulties, and multiple outcome predictions. An illustrative case study on a widely accepted scientific argumentation framework, ALARM, is provided to demonstrate the efficacy of the proposed approach.

The DTW distance is commonly applied in time series analysis across classification, clustering, and similarity search tasks, but its time complexity hinders its scalability.
