In random systems, the scattering matrix correlates incident wave patterns with internal distributions within a volume, and previously this correlation was leveraged to increase energy delivered to a target. This study determines a general set of constraints and formulas governing the eigenvalues and modes within any given scattering setup - including complex geometries, and broad categories such as slabs and narrow channels. Our mathematical framework reveals limitations and correlations for intensity within system boundaries, and derived properties apply universally to different types and strengths of wave, and multiple wave types.

Researchers have identified the far-side counterpart to a well-studied spiral arm in the center of the Milky Way, which is observed expanding. This far-side arm, detected through carbon monoxide emissions, can be followed in a map of Galactic longitude and velocity as a faint feature extending at least 20 degrees. Both the far-side and near-side arms exhibit comparable features including velocities, widths, heights, and mass distribution. Based on further investigation using 21-cm data, it's found that these spiral arms are primarily composed of molecular gas. This new evidence lends support to the presence of a bar structure at the center of the Galaxy and should aid in understanding its properties.

Increasingly, optimization methods are being employed to uncover a broad range of solutions. Our comparison across multi-objective optimization, multimodal optimization, and quality diversity in a straightforward context reveals that multi-objective optimization may not consistently generate significant diversity. By contrast, multimodal optimization tends to yield solutions with superior fitness levels. Meanwhile, quality diversity proves to be resilient to genetic neutrality and yields the most diverse set of solutions overall. Furthermore, integrating an autoencoder allows for the automated discovery of phenotypic features, which, in conjunction with quality diversity, facilitates the creation of a more extensive and diverse solution set. Ultimately, we offer strategic guidance on the appropriate application of these optimization techniques.

The Stable Roommates problem concerns pairing a set of agents according to their individual preference lists with specific hierarchical rankings. A key condition for any established pairings is that they must remain stable - preventing the situation where two agents would prefer each other over their respective matches. Variants of the Stable Roommates problem, including those involving larger groups of agents and distinct valuation methods, offer alternative scenarios for exploring agent matchings. A more complex form of the Stable Roommates problem, incorporating additively separable valuations and three-dimensional groupings, was explored, revealing instances where no stable matches exist and a direct approach is NP-complete, even when using limited binary valuations. However, we found that, under the condition of binary and symmetric valuations, any feasible 2-approximation algorithm can be developed into an optimal one. Additionally, we presented criteria for determining when a specific matching is stable, as well as conditions under which an agent's most preferred match in a stable pairing must also be their match.

Our research systematically explores how different mechanisms of electron-phonon
interaction affect valley behavior in two-dimensional materials. When we restrict
our study to constant strain conditions, we observe that two mechanisms, cone tilt
and deformation potential, yield analogous effects on valley Hall responses.
However, this equivalence does not apply when the coupling involves position-dependent
velocity of electrons. Under these conditions, valley Hall effect is robust against
changes in carrier density in the unconstrained scenario. Additionally, our findings
also shed light on the interplay between valley Hall effect and the 2D valley Hall
conductivity, shedding new light on the emerging features in both scenarios.
Furthermore, our analysis addresses the impact of pseudospin pseudomomentum on
electron-phonon interactions and their consequences.

We examine the class of all metric spaces with their distances measured by Gromov--Hausdorff distance. The subsets of spaces with bounded distances are called clouds, representing maximal subclasses within this group. Scaling the distances of a space by a positive factor yields a transformed metric space, belonging to the same Gromov--Hausdorff class. This type of transformation can cause some clouds to jump into others, as noted in our previous study. To explain this phenomenon, we investigated the stability of these space transformations. This paper demonstrates that any cloud having non-deformed transformations is unique and resides at the center of the Gromov--Hausdorff class. Additionally, we present the complete classification of 1-dimensional spaces, including their cloud decompositions, and provide an overview of the remaining open problems in this field.

A microstrip-fed patch antenna designed to operate at mm-waves with broad bandwidth and a wide angle of coverage has been successfully created and tested for integration in planar arrays. The designed antenna has a significant bandwidth of 13.1%, operating between 34.1 GHz and 38.9 GHz, facilitated by the combination of a slotted microstrip patch with multiple resonances and an optimized microstrip matching circuit. Constructed using the low-cost RO3003 substrate, this antenna exhibits broad coverage and wide coverage angles due to its built-in microstrip reflex microstrip patch geometry, which includes parallel microstrip refractors for even broader patterns. The geometric simplicity and wide angle of coverage make this antenna suitable for mm-wave communication applications, including phased arrays and conformal array implementations.

Large-scale, fault-tolerant quantum computing relies heavily on topological error correction codes due to their ability to adapt to faulty operations. Although fault-tolerant decoding algorithms have been developed, the high computational complexity of these methods threatens to surpass the capabilities of the classical processing units in the near future. To mitigate this issue, researchers have recently proposed the use of reinforcement learning techniques to accelerate the decoding process, yielding promising results in practical decoding scenarios. This study provides an in-depth review of the latest developments in reinforcement learning decoding, covering topics such as the adoption of neural reinforcement learning, the development of new fault-tolerant decoding algorithms, and the implementation of error correction schemes. Our analysis includes an examination of the decoding efficiency and scalability of these methods, along with a discussion of the promising prospects and potential future applications of reinforcement learning in quantum computing.

Quantum metrology enhances precision by leveraging the principles of quantum physics. This can be accomplished through interferometry, by first manipulating highly entangled quantum states before collecting information about an unknown variable through single measurements. Although this typically yields the most effective outcome, applying this method is extremely difficult when dealing with larger states. Another approach is offered by quantum jump metrology, a method that extracts information by continuously monitoring an open quantum system and inducing correlations with the assistance of quantum feedback control. This method is utilised to study the measurement of relative phases in optical systems consisting of two interconnected cavities, and controlled by quantum feedback from laser pulses. The approach is shown to reach a precision superior to the standard quantum precision limit, without needing highly complex quantum states and with greater scalability than traditional interferometry.

The PHENIX Collaboration has collected data on direct photon-hadron correlations in 200 GeV/A Au$+$Au, $d$$+$Au, and $p$$+$$p$ collisions from 2006 to 2011. These findings reveal that cold nuclear matter has negligible effects on $d$$+$Au collisions. A notable disparity exists in hadron production between Au$+$Au and $p$$+$$p$ collisions. Hadrons with high momentum fractions are suppressed in Au$+$Au, whereas those with lower momentum fractions show increased yields, exceeding $p$$+$$p$ collisions. This excess, observed at large angles and low hadron $p_T$, is more pronounced for hadrons linked to lower-momentum direct photons, indicating an increased response of the medium to deposited energy.

In this hybrid digital-analog approach to quantum computing, any quantum algorithm can be implemented without traditional two-qubit gates by utilizing an inherent, always-active connection between qubits. Building on this principle, our research explores how digital-analog simulation can be used to study fermionic systems, specifically the Fermi-Hubbard model, using a fermionic SWAP network and a method to correct distortions. Focusing on the effects of qubit connectivity and the distribution of interaction coefficients, as well as the precision of entanglement-inducing operations, our results indicate that an optimal qubit connectivity arrangement for simulating fermionic systems of any dimensionality is a chain for systems without spin and a ladder for those with spin. This relatively straightforward connectivity arrangement makes the digital-analog method particularly appealing for fermionic quantum simulations.

A common issue in machine learning lies in striking a balance between optimizing performance and robustly handling out-of-distribution (OoD) scenarios. Certain methods rely on complex penalty terms that can be difficult to optimize, as they either over- or under-penalize the model's predictions. 

We introduce an approach that begins with networks initialized using a comprehensive feature set, allowing even basic models to achieve improved performance. On one hand, this rich representation provides an effective starting point for the optimizer, while on the other hand, it incorporates a beneficial bias that helps handle OoD situations.

This robust feature set is generated using the Rich Feature Construction (RFC) algorithm, which combines backward elimination with data-efficient estimation techniques. The algorithm is adaptable to various kernel types and efficiently produces high-quality features, even for large-scale datasets. 

Using RFC, we achieved state-of-the-art results on multiple OoD benchmarks and demonstrated the benefits of enhancing models with this feature set through our experiments.

Achieving the formation of intricate structures and rapid concentration of light within or through biological tissues are significant challenges in the field of opto-biology. We have developed a novel system featuring a rapid, high-resolution liquid crystal display that can quickly create and adjust multiple 3D patterns in tissues with fast response times. Our system enables the rapid formation and customization of various shapes within tissues, as well as the rapid accumulation of high-intensity light within tissues. We have successfully demonstrated the use of our system to achieve intricate structures in a cell culture, as well as to enhance the image quality of tissues through the accurate distribution of scattered light.

We appreciate the discussion opportunity facilitated by editors and valuable input from discussants. Our work is influenced by the inspiring research of Kallus (2020), which enhances policy learning efficiency via retargeting. Building upon Dukes and Vansteelandt (2020), we distinguish our research from Kallus (2020) in Section 1 by highlighting their distinct assumptions, variations, and research objectives. In Section 2, guided by Li et al. (2020) and Liang and Zhao (2020), we analyze the efficient policy evaluation problem using data from both the training and testing distributions. Our results demonstrate that under specific growth conditions, efficient value function estimates can yield strong performance, although connections with the existing literature reveal limitations under slower testing sample size growth. In contrast, the testing sample size requirement for DRITR is more relaxed than that of efficient policy evaluation using combined data. In Section 3, we emphasize the broad applicability and utility of DRITR.

Monolithic CMOS sensors featuring small collection electrodes are advantageous due to high signal quality and low power consumption. However, these sensors have limited functionality due to the use of thin high-resistivity epitaxial layers during fabrication. In this study, researchers investigate the active sensor depth using the CLICTD technology, a small collection-electrode monolithic demonstrator. Particle beams are utilized to analyze the charge collection properties and device performance. Various sensor thicknesses are examined, and comparisons are made with simulated results. Furthermore, the study evaluates the use of a full planar CMOS process on a high-resistivity substrate.

Advanced telescopes strive to spot planets at closer distances, lower masses, or older ages than ever before, with the ultimate goal of directly identifying habitable-zone planets with masses similar to those of Earth. Despite recent technological improvements, a significant barrier remains, with the ability of current high-tech ground-based telescopes limited by image speckles that obstruct our view. This problem has been extensively studied, yet no satisfactory solution has been implemented on a large scale. Recently, fast atmospheric self-coherent camera (FAST) technology was introduced as a promising approach to mitigate the effect of speckles and enhance the image quality of future telescopes. Here, we present the first results of employing FAST in a real-world setting within the Santa Cruz Extreme Adaptive Optics Laboratory Testbed. Our data showcases the capability of FAST to function at the level of individual pixels, thereby eliminating speckle noise and allowing for the clear observation of various astronomical objects with reduced noise. Our experiments successfully demonstrated the potential of FAST to observe a planet transiting across a larger dimension, thereby retaining nearly the entire flux of the planet as it moves in and out of our view.

This study presents a novel exogenous model to tackle the challenge of negative interest rates, maintaining the mathematical ease of the Cox-Ingersoll-Ross model, and accurately replicating the observed yield curve. It combines the difference between two separate Cox-Ingersoll-Ross processes, one representing the nominal interest rate and another representing the differential adjustment for negative rates. The inclusion of the difference ensures the nominal rate remains above its limiting boundary at zero. Our approach employs the classical Heston framework, incorporating two separate mean-reverting processes for volatility and correlation. Numerical evaluations via Monte-Carlo simulations are carried out to demonstrate variational approximations, utilizing the Ky-Fan maximum theorem to determine optimal boundary adjustments for negative rates. Additionally, this research compares various distributional negative rate scenarios, including normal, skew-normal, and Student's t distributions.

Research into the characteristics of neutrino oscillations when neutrinos travel longer distances is essential in uncovering the properties of eV-scale sterile neutrinos. The DUNE experiment, set up to study such oscillations, has considerable potential in exploring this region of mass, as predicted by multiple models. The DUNE potential can be examined through two main areas: neutral-current interactions and purely leptonic interactions. The DUNE potential can be calculated based on a range of assumptions regarding the creation of sterile neutrinos. The DUNE potential can reach a limit of $10^{-18}$ erg/cm$^2$ erg in a study of a few years' duration, making it a comprehensive investigation into the properties of sub-eV sterile neutrinos in a wide range of theoretical frameworks.

When analyzing mixed-effects meta-regressions, assumptions about independence and equal variances may not always hold. In such cases, robust estimators are available but their performance has not been extensively evaluated, particularly when heterogeneity involves both between-study and within-study components. To address this gap, we calculate the asymptotic covariance matrix for a cluster-robust meta-regression model that accounts for both types of variance. Subsequently, we derive unbiased estimators for their components using consistent estimation. By applying this framework, we investigate the performance of various estimators, including those for their asymptotic standard errors, under realistic sample sizes and diverse scenarios of heterogeneity. The findings suggest that the Newcombe-Selke and Crowther estimators excel, offering superior accuracy and bias performance compared to other alternatives, especially when standard assumptions about heterogeneity hold.

This study introduces an advanced integration method for simulating multiple steps of particle collisions in flows. Currently, numerical simulations of particle collisions typically rely on an ad-hoc timescale derived from kinetic theory, but this approach can lead to unrealistic physical predictions, especially at higher particle concentrations. We have developed a new integration technique that utilizes the particles' actual collision time, measured directly from their velocities and positions, thereby addressing the long-standing issue of incorrect timescales in particle simulation models. To validate our method, we have conducted comprehensive simulations of three complex systems: a binary particle collision, a particle colliding with a wall, and a particle collision occurring in a flowing fluid environment. The results of these tests clearly demonstrate the superiority of our new algorithm over existing models.

Investigating the source of radiation energy in the Unruh/Hawking process has shed new light on the particle number definition, particularly as it relates to conservation laws. Research has found that particle radiation is not a product of gravitational force-driven pair creation, but rather an outcome stemming from disparities in the laws governing particle number definition. In the far distant future, the source of emitted energy corresponds to zero-point fluctuations characterized by exponentially large wave numbers, prompting a reassessment of the black hole evaporation paradigm.

The effect of transverse momentum broadening on parton propagation through a large nucleus is investigated using various models in the color dipole framework. These models generate different values of a key coefficient that influence broadening calculations. Results obtained via numerical analysis are then compared with LHCb and ALICE experimental findings for nuclear broadening in the context of lead-lead collisions at various center-of-mass energies. It is observed that models that accurately replicate small-to-medium energy data often fail to do so at higher energies, specifically in situations where a significant number of partons are produced. However, models that account for parton recombination mechanisms perform better at reproducing experimental data, particularly at LHC energies where parton recombination is anticipated to have a substantial impact.

This article presents $2$ distinct proof methodologies establishing the existence of pairs of relatively prime positive integers, $a$ and $b$, for which the following congruence is satisfied: the expression $a^2+ab+b^2$ can be factored as $7$ raised to a power of $n$.

The video explores the dynamics of a liquid jet that enters a channel filled with the same fluid. As the jet interacts with the surrounding stream, it becomes encircled by a sheath of entrained air. This sheath plays a significant role in the dynamic behavior of the jet and its penetration into the stream. Additionally, we examine the instability effects that develop on the liquid jet and the consequences of these effects on its behavior in the context of fluid dynamics.

High-performance computing systems rely heavily on fault tolerance to prevent data loss and ensure system reliability. Recent advances in non-volatile memory have made it feasible to achieve this, as data in such memory is preserved even during crashes. While conventional error detection and recovery methods in NVM require manual intervention, these can be partially handled by the memory itself, simplifying the process for programmers. Our focus is on providing automatic crash consistency for high-performance computing applications, specifically those using checkpoint-verify-restart (CVR) techniques. This involves studying the behavior of algorithmic components to minimize memory access fragmentation during checkpointing, as excessive full pages can hinder performance. By analyzing the characteristics of double precision floating-point operations common in computational science, we developed the fast-CVR solution, integrating error detection and recovery directly into the memory and eliminating the need for manual coding. Compared to existing fast-CVR implementations, our approach enhances performance by up to 30% while also enhancing portability across diverse algorithms and new, emerging applications.

Organizational frameworks like information hierarchies are commonly used to present complex data and simplify navigation, yet the automatic generation methods available today don't account for the interconnections in modern information networks. Presently, most techniques represent topics as abstract probabilities rather than tangible components of the underlying network, and many lack the scalability needed for web-based applications. In contrast, we propose a novel approach, Hierarchical Document Topic Model (HDTM), utilizing a non-parametric distributed processing model that effectively extracts meaningful hierarchies from large networks, even at a massive data scale, as evidenced by our experiments using three smaller datasets and a large Wikipedia ensemble.

We conducted an exhaustive examination comparing the statistical properties of non-hierarchical three-body systems with corresponding theoretical models. By running and analyzing one million simulations for diverse initial conditions, both with and without equal masses in three-body systems, we were able to achieve precise statistical accuracy. Four distinct measures were used to characterize the distribution of ergodic disintegrations: the probability of escape for individual bodies, the exponent representing narrow escapes, the predicted absorption as a function of binary energy and angular momentum, and the distribution of lifetimes. Our results showed that escape probabilities matched theoretical predictions with high precision, marking a significant improvement over previous statistical theories. Furthermore, the measured values of the exponent near marginally unbound escape thresholds agreed well with an independent, flux-based prediction. Both findings support the flux-based three-body statistical framework, and our measurements of absorptivity and lifetime distributions provide valuable resources for further testing and validation of statistical models.

Measurements of the nuclear modification factors of J/$\psi$ and $\psi$(2S) mesons were made in collisions of lead ions at the Large Hadron Collider in 2015. The study was based on data from both lead-lead and proton-proton collisions, involving energies of 5.02 TeV for lead-lead and 5.02 TeV for proton-proton collisions. The nuclear modification factors for J/$\psi$ were found to be 3.08 in central collisions and 0.94 in peripheral collisions, while the nuclear modification factors for $\psi$(2S) were 4.99 in central collisions and 1.26 in peripheral collisions. The study also found the suppression to be more pronounced for $\psi$(2S) than J/$\psi$, which is in agreement with expectations.

We propose an arrangement of predicates in continuous logic such that the
logical framework's meaning can be structured within a hyperdoctrine framework.
This hyperdoctrine can be incorporated into a hyperdoctrine representing subobjects within a suitable category of topological structures. 
To achieve this incorporation, we first simplify the hyperdoctrine framework for continuous logic and establish an equivalence between its category of equivalence relations and that of complete metric spaces under uniform mappings.

When designing a software system, a modification in one component may
unintentionally impact other parts, hindering overall system performance. This is
addressed by conducting regression testing, which re-evaluates system sections
aimed at preventing adverse effects. However, pinpointing these affected areas
proves challenging, making it essential to identify system changes through a
different approach. We apply singular value decomposition to group software
modifications by their functional roles, allowing for more efficient detection
of areas requiring retesting during subsequent updates. By leveraging parallel
calculations on shared memory systems, we enhance testing speed, ensuring optimal
results can be obtained even as software systems scale up.

A new technique is proposed to forecast suicidal ideation based on the integration of Electronic Health Records and Ecological Momentary Assessment data utilizing advanced deep sequential models. These datasets consist of asynchronous, variable-length, randomly sampled sequences which are modelled separately using Recurrent Neural Networks and combined through the alignment of hidden states, along with attention and pre-training schemes to handle differing sequence lengths. Experimental outcomes using 1023 patients' data demonstrate that the incorporation of Ecological Momentary Assessment records significantly increases the recall of the model in predicting suicidal ideation, from 48.13% using Electronic Health Record data alone to 67.78%. Furthermore, the proposed method offers enhanced interpretability through dimensionality reduction in the latent space and medical feature analysis.

Our research reports a significant $\sim 5\sigma$ discovery of polarized X-ray emission within a range of 0.5-2.5 keV from Cassiopeia A with IXPE. This finding stems from an integrated 1.06 million-second observation. By integrating over the neutron star's emission and other contaminants, we found a significant polarization of $1.8 \pm 0.3$ percent from a range of 0.5-2.5 keV. This emission is predominantly powered by the slowing down secondary electrons, producing polarized synchrotron radiation. This discovery confirms earlier findings from Bepo and KAIROS observations of polarized X-rays from Cassiopeia A, yielding a consistent lower energy bound of ~0.5 keV for synchrotron radiation. This energy suggests a containment volume of ~300 pc$^3$ for the primary forward shock, complementary to earlier estimates. This emission is subject to energy loss due to inverse Compton scattering in a rough approximation, leading to an observed polarization ratio decrease by a factor of $\sim 2$. Additionally, we note that further detailed simulations incorporating both synchrotron and IC scattering are needed to thoroughly explain the observed polarization, along with consideration of energy input from reacceleration.

Consider a set $\{a_1, \ldots, a_n\}$ of distinct positive integers where $a_1 < \ldots < a_n$, with the requirement that only subset sums up to a size of at most $\lambda n$ be unique. Erdos originally proposed a conjecture suggesting that $a_n > c \cdot 2^n$, with the current record at $a_n > c \cdot 2^n/\sqrt{n}$. This article presents modified constraints where we investigate lower and upper bounds for the minimum possible value of the largest element $a_n$ in various scenarios.

The characteristics of dense matter within the density range of 1-10 times nuclear saturation density, present in compact stars, are intriguingly ambiguous and may influence neutron star dynamics as detected via gravitational waves.  As a compact star's density increases, sound velocity approaches the conformal limit at high densities, satisfying the causality limit while its detailed behavior remains disputed. It's hypothesized that dense matter sound velocity can be an indicator of a deconfinement phase transition, possibly exhibiting a distinctive relationship with density. Our work delves into the fundamental properties of dense matter sound velocity and the adiabatic index within neutron stars, quark stars, and hybrid stars.  By simulating the hadron-quark phase transition with different interface tension, we found the sound velocity's expected behavior could also be achieved without altering the source star's composition.  Therefore, the sound velocity's slope at nuclear saturation density can be an indicator of the compact star's equation of state while its absolute value can reveal the existing matter's degree of baryonization.  Additionally, our findings indicate the sound velocity's absolute value can be up to 1.35, depending on the baryon composition, potentially explaining the upper limit of sound velocity's observed value in compact stars.  Lastly, our research shows the sound velocity's possible existence in compact stars can facilitate stellar structure's understanding and the identification of the quark deconfinement phase transition.

We investigate a variety of non-classical states made up of superposed, both squeezed and displaced number states, examining their phase space structure in relation to Heisenberg limited sensitivity in parameter estimation. Certain combinations of squeezing and displacement are identified that maintain over 99% state fidelity compared to a highly sensitive reference state, known as a compass state, which also exhibits equivalent variance in small shifts measurements. Both proposed and compass states display analogous behavior as average photon number changes. Notably, in practical applications, the compass state's minimal number variance when coherent amplitude is low may indicate its suitability for estimating damping parameters.

During gas-liquid interfaces that are subject to irregular movement such as splashing and atomization, the resulting fluid structures can be intricate and embedded in their surroundings. In this work, we employ a technique called skeletonization to extract the fundamental information needed to represent their geometry. By applying this method to simulations of a breaking liquid jet, we successfully obtain the topological features of the interface, thereby differentiating and quantifying the resulting liquid clusters. Furthermore, we propose an extension to the classic definition of genus called $g_{\omega}$. This new concept incorporates the winding number of the interface and facilitates the identification of closed loops even after the partitioning of the interface.

Researchers discovered that certain influenza viruses exhibit active movement on surfaces with carbohydrate layers by rolling along them, as shown in recent studies. This phenomenon was previously proposed to be an example of viral surface metabolism, where the collection of spike proteins interacts with the carbohydrates, generating mechanical movement through a self-organizing process. This research aims to investigate in greater detail the physical aspects underlying this rolling motion, developing a theory that explains the motor's behavior, as well as validating the results using simulations to analyze the impact of various factors. The outcomes of this study strongly indicate that viral movement on surfaces is statistically certain to occur when the virus exhibits enzymatic activity.

We examined over 8,000 massive, edge-on disk galaxies from the SDSS dataset, focusing on two types: S and U galaxies. Our analysis revealed that U galaxies have distinct characteristics, including bluer optical colors and higher star formation rates, compared to S galaxies. U galaxies, particularly those with more extreme warping, exhibited higher star formation rates. Contrary to expectations, U galaxies in groups and clusters do not show a correlation with the tidal force exerted by their nearest neighbor. However, U galaxies are more common in groups and clusters and share similarities with 'jellyfish' galaxies formed through ram-pressure stripping (RPS). This led us to suggest that RPS could be a potential mechanism explaining the presence of U galaxies in groups and clusters.

This research focuses on harmonic functions within the context of a particular type of manifold where the Ricci curvature decreases over time and the scalar curvature remains constant. We have derived a key theorem demonstrating that bounded harmonic functions are constant in this specific type of manifold, without relying on an established growth estimate. Consequently, this result implies that the set of all harmonic functions that grow at a polynomial rate on these manifolds is finite-dimensional.

Compounds composed of potassium ($A=$ K, Rb, Cs) combined with boron in a 2:1 ratio, exhibit unique cubic structures called the Laves phase with a specific Fd$\bar{3}$m symmetry. The arrangement of atoms within these crystals permits the existence of chirally behaving phonons, which correspond to atoms circling their equilibrium positions. Given that inversion symmetry and time reversal symmetry govern the total pseudo-angular momentum of the system, this momentum is zero. By introducing dopants, researchers find that this can result in a new crystal structure, F$\bar{4}3$m. Novel materials, KRbBi$_{4}$ and RbCsBi$_{4}$, exhibit no dynamic instability; the inversion symmetry disruption however, leads to phonons with a non-zero total pseudo-angular momentum. Chirally behaving phonons emerge at specific points within the Brillouin zone. The condition allowing the phonon to be chiral - absence of inversion and mirror symmetry - is fulfilled by these phonons. The total pseudo-angular momentum of the system becomes finite, stemming from the phonon's total momentum. By using first principles calculations, researchers find that this phenomenon occurs in Bi$^{3-}$ ion polarizability, causing a dynamic instability in Bi$^{3-}$ system. The chiral phonons result in an asymmetrical potential well for dopants within the potential well. The potential application of chiral phonons in controlling dopant

In insulators, Born effective charges relate to how the positioning of individual atomic sublattices generates electric polarization. Our investigation extends this concept to metals and calculates non-adiabatic Born effective charges in two-dimensional massive Dirac fermion systems. Our results show that, unlike in insulators, Born effective charges in metals depend on the exchange rate between the kinetic energy of electrons and the external electromagnetic field frequency. Additionally, our findings connect Born effective charges in metals to their Drude response.

We are reassessing the significance of thermal fluctuations in incompressible fluid turbulence and determining their relevance on a particular scale. As earlier research by Betchov predicted decades ago, this scale is equivalent to the Kolmogorov length, although it's still many orders of magnitude greater than the average free path. This finding suggests that the non-random, or deterministic, form of the Navier-Stokes equation is insufficient for modeling the turbulence dissipation range, and therefore, the current understanding of this range needs to be revised. We provide mathematical proofs for this conclusion within the framework of high-Reynolds number turbulence and its generalizations. We also provide experimental verification of the findings by analyzing data from the US Third International Air Sea Interaction Data Swamp project.

Three-dimensional topological insulators can be identified by a magnetoelectric coefficient with a quantized value, but it lacks observable properties because it requires an external magnetic field for a response. We're proposing an extension of this concept, the topological magnetoelectric effect, where a time-reversal symmetric interaction occurs between the external electric and magnetic fields and the intrinsic electric and magnetic fields of a topological insulator. This new interaction has been shown to relate to a nonlinear version of the Witten effect and can be seen as a form of a half integer quantum Hall effect that occurs within a thin film made from a topological insulator.

In systems featuring delayed nonlinearity, we observe chaotic diffusion as a typical trait, where it is found that modulating the time delay periodically leads to a significant enhancement of the diffusion coefficient by several orders of magnitude, especially when the modulation's map exhibits mode locking, characteristic of laminar chaos. For the first time, we establish a link between Arnold tongue patterns in parameter space and the diffusive behavior of delay systems. Contrary to expectation, this increase in diffusion is accompanied by a considerable decrease in the system's effective dimensionality.

We provide rigorous definitions for sound and sufficient denotational and operational interpretations of the stochastic lambda calculus. By adapting established techniques to reason about high-level probabilistic code, this study achieves a breakthrough in linking operational and denotational views with a proven adequacy theorem, thereby closing a key outstanding issue identified in earlier work (Bacci et al., 2018).

Discussions among developers encompass a variety of interactions, including in-person conversations and online comments, which are beneficial to analyze to gain insight into the design process. This is particularly crucial in the context of bug reports, where the discussion section often provides valuable context missed by current analysis methods. Although conventional design review methods focus on individual issues, they overlook the broader implications of design decisions. This leads to inconsistent application of these decisions, known as design review instability. This paper proposes a new approach, called DesignReview, which leverages machine learning to automatically identify stable design decisions from relevant discussion data, encompassing both text and timing information. DesignReview's effectiveness is demonstrated in a case study involving data from the Bugzilla issue tracking system.

A proposed model explains the existence of gravity, dark energy, and dark matter.
Dark energy and dark matter stem from a false vacuum state's random energy fluctuations, characterized by large-scale negative and short-scale positive pressures, respectively, representing incoherent and coherent aspects of a superfluid/supersolid state.
Gravity emerges from topological defects within the post-inflation virtual "condensate" component.
Consequently, it is anticipated that exotic particles that could explain dark matter will not be detected at the LHC.
Moreover, it is suggested that the de Sitter horizon associated with holographic dark energy acts as a complete absorber in the Penrose-Tralfalgarborg model, limiting the entropy of the universe and potentially resolving the cosmological constant problem.

Proximal methods can efficiently uncover the underlying pattern in nonsmooth optimization problems, and, in many cases, identifying this structure is a valuable byproduct. Our goal is to develop a protocol that extracts the submanifolds on which the proximal gradient method converges and utilizes this information to accelerate convergence to critical points along these paths. Moreover, our protocol can also be used to discover the natural gradients on these submanifolds, and our experimental findings validate its effectiveness.

We are introducing a new concept called weakly $1$-absorbing prime ideals within a commutative ring with identity, which is an ideal containing at least two nonzero elements whose product is a nonzero divisor. This new idea complements the concept of weakly prime ideals. Our research provides properties and characterizations of weakly $1$-absorbing prime ideals, along with an examination of their relationships with prime ideals, weakly prime ideals, and universally weakly $1$-absorbing prime ideals. Additionally, we have derived a complete classification of weakly $1$-absorbing prime ideals in finite commutative rings. Our study further identifies some inherent flaws in the existing literature and provides corrections to related results.

We present new findings for two semileptonic decay processes, $B^0$ decaying into $\rho^-$ and a lepton-neutrino pair, and $B^+$ decaying into $\rho^0$ with the same pair, utilizing data from Belle II's sample equivalent to 189.9/fb, collected using the SuperKEKB $e^-e^+$ collider. To identify these decays, the research involved reconstructing the full recoil B-meson within hadronic end products, after which the researchers computed total branching ratios by performing statistical fits on missing mass square and dipion mass in the candidate signal, determining the former to be $4.12 \pm 0.64 (stat.) \pm 1.16 (syst.) \times 10^{-4}$ and the latter as $1.77 \pm 0.23 (stat.) \pm 0.36 (syst.) \times 10^{-4}$. These findings are primarily subject to systematic error due to nonresonant influences on B-meson decay patterns.

Our team employed photonic technology to revolutionize the conventional method of spectroscopy, enabling on-device spectral cross-correlation using a template spectrum. This was achieved by designing photonic devices with intricately modulated transmission spectra, thus performing cross-correlation without the need for dispersion. Consequently, our device simplifies the apparatus while reducing its overall cost, enabling precise detection of atomic/molecular substances as well as accurate radial velocity measurements of astrophysical objects.

We outline two innovative design approaches based on distinct photonic platforms, silicon and fibre-based photonics. Silicon-based photonic technology incorporates thermally modulated ring resonators for spectral cross-correlation, whereas fibre-based photonics utilize strain-modulated customized fibre Bragg gratings. Both approaches successfully detected molecular gas in a laboratory setting and are currently undergoing field testing.

Furthermore, our research has far-reaching implications as these photonic devices may pave the way for developing low-cost, custom-built spectrographic instruments capable of simultaneously analyzing multiple objects or providing high-resolution field spectra. This technology has immense potential to contribute to groundbreaking research in stellar radial velocity measurements and exoplanet discoveries.

In the last few years, various machine learning models have emerged with the aim of tackling polypharmacy side effects, predicting medication interactions, and optimizing combination therapies. This paper takes a comprehensive approach, offering a theoretical framework that can address these challenges through relational machine learning models. It provides key concepts, assesses existing model architectures, discusses relevant evaluation metrics, datasets, and testing protocols. Furthermore, it highlights significant potential applications and suggests vital research paths for the future in this field.

Several local authorities face challenges in deploying advanced automated
evaluation of road damage due to a lack of necessary technology, expertise, and
financial resources. While countries like Japan and the UK have made significant
progress in using computer vision to assess road condition, this technique has
not been widely adopted by other nations. Japan and the UK have access to
specialized equipment and skilled personnel, but what if we were to combine their
resources? A crucial step towards enhancing global road assessment capabilities
is integrating knowledge from distinct countries and applying it to new, unseen
roads. This research delves into the field of hyperspectral image analysis for
road assessment, with an emphasis on discovering new patterns and learning
combinations of features. We're exploring whether a multi-country database can
be utilized for evaluating road damage, with results indicating that, indeed,
knowledge from Japan and the UK can be leveraged to detect damage on Dutch roads.

Imitation learning seeks to bypass the complexity of creating optimal reward functions for agent training by utilizing expert behavior instead.  The advantage of imitation learning over reinforcement learning is further amplified when obtaining accurate expert data is simplified.  Nevertheless, imitation learning typically relies on expert demonstrations within the same environment as the agents, which is often not feasible due to the vast scope of possible states in real-world settings.  In this research, we tackle the problem of obtaining expert data across different environments by utilizing the connections between expert states across these domains.  This approach, which utilizes multi-domain Variational Graphical Models to integrate expert data, enables the transfer of imitation learning techniques from one domain to another.  We provide extensive testing of this hypothesis across a variety of domain transitions and observation settings, which reveals that these models are capable of mimicking actions across diverse domains.  The resulting technique holds significant promise for applying imitation learning in diverse areas such as robotics and computer vision.

A major uncertainty in determining the initial mass function of the first (Population III) stars hinges on the ultimate fate of secondary protostars that form in the accretion disk - whether they will merge or remain separate. We concentrate on how the initial star formation was influenced by magnetic effects in a cosmological setting with existing magnetic fields. We conducted a series of simulations of magnetohydrodynamics, running up to 1000 years following the initial protostar formation. To represent the protostars and their magnetic field structures, we utilized a stiff equation of state approach instead of the conventional sink particle technique. Ten years after the initial protostar formation, we observed an amplification in magnetic field strength from picogauss to kilogauss in the region around protostars, matching that of contemporary stars. Due to the rapid orbital rotations in the vicinity of protostars, their magnetic field became increasingly wound up over the initial decade of protostar formation. As the accretion disk progressed to higher orbital speeds with time, the corresponding Lundquist number dropped, preventing further significant amplification of the magnetic field. Ultimately, in all of our simulations, the accretion disk fragmentation ceased 100-1000 years after the initial protostar formation due to the overwhelming effects of magnetohydrodynamic forces.
